md_docs_2live-media-input(3) Library Functions Manual md_docs_2live-media-input(3)

NAME

md_docs_2live-media-input - Open media during a session

In native mirror, client, and discovery sessions:

  • Press o (or Ctrl+O) to open an editable path/URL prompt.
  • Paste a URL or drop a file into the terminal to prefill that prompt.
  • Press v to prefill it from the clipboard, including a file copied in Explorer or Finder.
  • Press Enter to load the source or Escape to cancel.

The current source stays active while the replacement loads. A failed load retains the previous source. The centered editor and loading panel share the animated rainbow splash header. The loading panel remains until the new frame is ready, so the old source never flashes back after submission. Escape cancels a pending load; an external URL extractor may need to finish before another load can begin. Once loaded, Space pauses playback, the left and right arrow keys seek, and [** switches between media and the webcam. **<** and **> open the previous/next artifact from the beginning. At the ends of the list they do nothing. Finishing an artifact automatically opens the next; --loop repeats the complete playlist after the final artifact.

Drop additional files into the open prompt to append quoted paths on separate lines. Explorer's trailing separator space is removed, leaving the cursor directly after the closing quote. Enter plays the complete list in order.

The prompt accepts local paths, quoted paths, shell-escaped spaces, local file:// URIs, and URLs supported by the existing FFmpeg/yt-dlp resolver. Pasted content is never executed as a shell command.

Bracketed paste is the reliable automatic path. Some terminals insert dropped paths as ordinary keystrokes; complete path-shaped bursts are recognized too. When a terminal splits those keystrokes across reads, press o before dropping the file so every character goes into the prompt instead of session shortcuts.

Windows reads Unicode text and copied-file lists. macOS uses the system pasteboard. Linux uses wl-paste from wl-clipboard or xclip, including text/uri-list file selections. Clipboard access happens only when v is pressed. Multiple copied files become the same ordered playlist.

CLI input uses the same playlist model. Repeat --file and --url in playback order, including a mixture of both:

ascii-chat mirror --file "first video.mp4" --url "https://example.com/second.webm" --file "third.mp4"

A playlist supports up to 64 artifacts, each up to 255 UTF-8 bytes; the interactive editor accepts up to 8191 bytes of quoted text. Stdin (--file -) must be the only artifact. A failed replacement preserves the current source. The final artifact stays visible when playback ends. Snapshots and recording keep their configured session duration; skipping always opens a new decoder at the beginning.

Live input is polled independently of ASCII conversion. The FPS overlay counts newly acquired and successfully presented frames, including identical images; retained/paused redraws do not count.

Regression checks

Run the native playlist smoke test against the rebuilt binary:

python tests/integration/media_playlist.py --binary build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --artifacts build/playlist-smoke
python tests/integration/media_responsiveness.py --binary build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --artifacts build/pattern-response
python tests/integration/media_responsiveness.py --binary build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --webcam --artifacts build/webcam-response

Each responsiveness run renders for two minutes before measuring three open-prompt responses, with a 250 ms limit. The playlist test checks the rendered keyboard help, rainbow panels, cursor position, repeated drops, sequential EOF playback, looping, and previous/next restart behavior. These scripts require Python pyte, FFmpeg, and pexpect on POSIX; Pillow optionally saves terminal screenshots.

On Windows, media_audio_continuity.py additionally requires NumPy and PyAudioWPatch. Pass --binary, --Media, and --artifacts to compare actual speaker loopback against an FFmpeg-decoded reference. Captured audio stays in the local artifact directory.

To trace native frame freshness and verify the FPS overlay on every complete terminal update, run:

python tests/integration/live_frame_latency.py --binary build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --webcam --with-audio --duration 125 --check-input --artifacts build/live-frame-latency
python tests/integration/live_frame_latency.py --binary build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --webcam --fps 5 --duration 15 --artifacts build/throttled-camera
python tests/integration/frame_presentation.py --binary build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --artifacts build/frame-presentation

The first check also measures o responsiveness after sustained rendering. The throttled run checks that the camera backend discards queued old samples instead of replaying them. On Windows, CAMERA_FRAME logs include backlog relative to the fastest delivery and the driver timestamp's frame age when the driver supplies it (device_age_ms=-1 means unavailable). LIVE_FRAME separates acquisition, queue wait, conversion, and publication; FRAME_PRESENT measures submission through completed terminal output. These software timings do not measure monitor scanout or the camera's exposure time.

Native terminal backpressure and frame tracing

A completed stdout write does not mean a terminal frontend has displayed it. On a large terminal, each truecolor frame can be hundreds of KB. Sending the next frame as soon as Windows accepts the previous one lets a frontend accumulate old frames even when the C capture and presentation queues keep only the latest frame.

The native presenter sends an OSC 11 read-only color query after a fresh media frame. When the terminal supports this query, its reply establishes that the frontend has consumed the preceding output. Only one frame can await a reply; capture continues and replaces the latest mailbox snapshot while presentation waits. Input and modal screens remain responsive during that wait. FPS counts completed, acknowledged fresh frames; retained redraws never count. Terminals that do not answer the initial probe fall back to completed local writes.

The counter's seven cells on the first row are reserved during every media write. This keeps it visible while a terminal without synchronized output support draws parts of a frame, rather than erasing it and restoring it only after the art ends.

With --log-level Debug --log-file PATH, each frame now records acquisition and copy timing (CAMERA_FRAME, CAMERA_COPY), pipeline read/queue/conversion and publication (LIVE_FRAME), and completed output (FRAME_PRESENT, including capture_to_stdout_ms, geometry, composition, write, drain, dimensions and bytes). TERMINAL_ACK separately records frontend response and capture-to-frontend age. These measurements do not claim to measure monitor scanout.

The FPS check now uses a 286 by 73 terminal and checks intermediate 4 KB chunks, as well as complete frames and toggle-off behavior. The frontend emulator replies after parsing output, so its own rendering speed applies backpressure too:

python tests/integration/frame_presentation.py --binary build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --artifacts build/frame-presentation
python tests/integration/terminal_backpressure.py --binary build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --artifacts build/terminal-backpressure

The backpressure regression delays replies, holds one for 800 ms, verifies that no additional media frame is queued, checks responsive open-prompt input during the hold, and asserts that the FPS count follows actual completed presentations.

Timing a native webcam preview

For performance measurements, use an optimized build with symbols. The default Debug configuration deliberately disables optimization and inlining; it is useful for sanitizer checks, but adds significant cost to per-cell ANSI generation.

cmake --preset default -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
cmake --build build --target ascii-chat
build/bin/ascii-chat.exe --log-level debug --log-file build/frame-timings.log mirror --fps-counter
python tests/integration/frame_timing_report.py build/frame-timings.log

Keep the terminal frontend, viewport size, render mode, color mode, and machine load consistent when comparing runs. Measure the actual frontend, rather than substituting a hidden console or timing writes to a file. Compile before starting the measurement.

ASCII_STAGE separates allocation, resize, glyph/ANSI generation, and padding. FRAME_PRESENT includes the number of output chunks and the longest chunk's write time. The presenter combines the frontend query with the synchronized update's closing write; a supported frontend's reply replaces the redundant local console flush. Each media payload write is bounded to 64 KB so input can supersede an update between chunks.

The report retains the original capture-request-to-terminal measurement. It also joins frame IDs with camera sample timestamps to report sample-arrival-to-terminal age and, where available, camera-device-timestamp-to-terminal age. The latter includes the device age reported by Media Foundation. Unknown device timestamps are excluded. The coverage entry shows the capture interval retained in the log; check it because automatic log rotation can discard the start of a long run. These boundaries distinguish waiting for the next capture from processing a captured sample; none measures monitor scanout or independently verifies the camera's physical exposure timestamp.
